questions.:question/problem: Find the slope of the normal line to the curve $y = \sqrt{x} - 2$ at the point $(1,-1)$.
Find the slope of the normal line to the curve $y = 3x^{2} - 2x$ at the point $(2, 8)$.

questions.:question/worked-solution:
Let $f(x)={x}^{2}+3x.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
{f}^{'}(x)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}+3x)=2x+3
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(-1,-2):$

$$
m={f}^{'}(-1)=2(-1)+3=-2+3=1
$$

Therefore, the slope ${m}^{'}$ of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{'} & =-\frac{1}{m} \\  & =-\frac{1}{1} \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $f(x)=4-3{x}^{2}.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
{f}^{'}(x)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4-3{x}^{2})=-6x
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(1,1):$

$$
m={f}^{'}(1)=-6(1)=-6
$$

Therefore, the slope ${m}^{'}$ of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{'} & =-\frac{1}{m} \\  & =-\frac{1}{(-6)} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $f(x)=\frac{1}{4}{x}^{5}-4{x}^{2}.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
{f}^{'}(x)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\left(\frac{1}{4}{x}^{5}-4{x}^{2}\right)=\frac{5}{4}{x}^{4}-8x
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(2,-8):$

$$
m={f}^{'}(2)=\frac{5}{4}({2}^{4})-8(2)=20-16=4
$$

Therefore, the slope ${m}^{'}$ of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{'} & =-\frac{1}{m} \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $f(x)=2{x}^{3}-\frac{1}{{x}^{4}}.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\left(2{x}^{3}-\frac{1}{{x}^{4}}\right) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{3}-{x}^{-4}) \\  & =6{x}^{2}+4{x}^{-5} \\  & =6{x}^{2}+\frac{4}{{x}^{5}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(-1,-3):$

$$
m={f}^{'}(-1)=6{(-1)}^{2}+\frac{4}{(-1)^{5}}=6-4=2
$$

Therefore, the slope ${m}^{'}$ of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{'} & =-\frac{1}{m} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.:question/problem: Find the slope of the normal line to the curve $y=2{x}^{3}-x+3$ at the point $(1,4).$
questions.:question/worked-solution:
Let $f(x)=2{x}^{3}-x+3.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}(x)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{3}-x+3)=6{x}^{2}-1\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(1,4):$

$$
\begin{aligned}m={f}^{'}(1)=6(1)-1=5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line ${m}^{'}$ is

$$
{m}^{'}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{5}.
$$

questions.:question/problem: Find the slope of the normal line to the curve $y=2\sqrt{{x}^{3}}-2{x}^{2}$ at the point $(1,0).$
questions.:question/worked-solution:
Let $f(x)=2\sqrt{{x}^{3}}-2{x}^{2}.$ Computing the derivative ${f}^{′}(x)$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2\sqrt{{x}^{3}}-2{x}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{3/2}-2{x}^{2}) \\  & =3{x}^{1/2}-4x.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute ${f}^{′}(1)$, which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(1)=3(1)^{1/2}-4(1)=-1\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line ${m}^{′}$ is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=1.
$$

questions.:question/problem: Find the slope of the normal line to the curve $y={x}^{3}-4\sqrt{{x}^{5}}$ at the point $(1,-3).$
questions.:question/worked-solution:
Let $f(x)={x}^{3}-4\sqrt{{x}^{5}}.$ Computing the derivative ${f}^{′}(x)$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3}-4\sqrt{{x}^{5}}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3}-4{x}^{5/2}) \\  & =3{x}^{2}-10{x}^{3/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute ${f}^{′}(1)$, which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(1)=3(1)^{2}-10(1)^{3/2}=-7\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line  ${m}^{′}$ is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=\frac{1}{7}.
$$

questions.:question/problem: Find the slope of the normal line to the curve $y=\frac{2}{{x}^{5}}+7x$ at the point $(1,9).$
questions.:question/worked-solution:
Let $f(x)=\frac{2}{{x}^{5}}+7x.$ Computing the derivative ${f}^{′}(x)$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\left(\frac{2}{{x}^{5}}+7x\right) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{-5}+7x) \\  & =-10{x}^{-6}+7.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute ${f}^{′}(1)$, which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(1)=-10(1)^{-6}+7=-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line ${m}^{′}$ is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=\frac{1}{3}.
$$

Let $f(x)=4-\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\left(4-\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\right) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4-{x}^{-1/2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{x}^{3}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $\left(\frac{1}{4},2\right):$

$$
m={f}^{′}\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)}^{3}}}=4
$$

Therefore, the slope ${m}^{′}$ of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{′} & =-\frac{1}{m} \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.:question/problem: Find the slope of the normal line to the curve $y=\frac{1}{4{x}^{2}}+\frac{x}{2}$ at the point $\left(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{4}\right).$
questions.:question/worked-solution:
Let $f(x)=\frac{1}{4{x}^{2}}+\frac{x}{2}.$ Computing the derivative ${f}^{′}(x)$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\left(\frac{1}{4{x}^{2}}+\frac{x}{2}\right) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{-3}+\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute ${f}^{′}\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right),$ which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)=-\frac{1}{2}\cdot {\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)}^{-3}+\frac{1}{2}=\frac{9}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line ${m}^{′}$ is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{2}{9}.
$$

questions.:question/problem: Find the slope of the normal line to the curve $y=x^2-5x+1$ at the point $(1,-3)$.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
Let $f(x)=x^2-5x+1$. First, compute the derivative:

$$
f'(x)=2x-5.
$$

The slope of the tangent at $(1,-3)$ is

$$
m=f'(1)=2(1)-5=-3.
$$

The normal is perpendicular to the tangent, so its slope is the negative reciprocal:

$$
m'=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{-3}=\frac{1}{3}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(x)&=\frac{x^2-2x+1}{x^{1/2}}\\
&=x^{3/2}-2x^{1/2}+x^{-1/2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Apply the power rule to all three terms:

$$
f'(x)=\frac{3}{2}x^{1/2}-x^{-1/2}-\frac{1}{2}x^{-3/2}.
$$

The slope of the tangent at $\left(4,\frac{9}{2}\right)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}
m=f'(4)&=\frac{3}{2}\sqrt{4}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{4}}-\frac{1}{2(4)^{3/2}}\\
&=3-\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{16}\\
&=\frac{39}{16}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The normal has the negative reciprocal slope:

$$
m'=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{39/16}=-\frac{16}{39}.
$$

Let $f(x)=(x+1)(x^2-2x)$. Expand before differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}

\end{aligned}

canonical_example.:question/problem: Find the slope of the normal line to the curve $y = 2x^3 -x^2$ at the point $(1,1).$
canonical_example.:question/worked-solution:
Let $f(x) = 2x^3-x^2.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
f'(x)  =6x^2 -2x
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(1,1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
m=f'(1) = 6(1)^2 - 2(1) = 4
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line $m'$ is

$$
m' = -\dfrac{1}{m} = -\dfrac 1 4.
$$
